Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Coventry City and Newcastle United from the Ricoh Arena. Newcastle have played only once there in the league – a 4-1 victory in the Championship back in 2010 when Chris Hughton’s side stormed the league. Their last top-flight visit to the city was way back in 2000, the year Cov’s 34-season spell in the top division ended. Alan Shearer Kevin Gallacher scored at Highfield Road on that occasion, a year after they were sent packing 4-1 by Gordon Strachan’s side by virtue of goals from Carlton Palmer, Paul Williams, Robbie Keane and Mustapha Hadji.

Today’s visit begins with Newcastle in 11th, having bounced back from their Monday night mauling at Elland Road to beat Hull 23 days ago. So bunched is the table, though, that victory tonight would propel them up to fourth. Coventry, by contrast, are 19th after one win and four defeats from their opening five games. If they win they would join Manchester United on six points and leap to 14th, one place ahead of Nottingham Forest, the team they beat last time out before the international break.

Frank Lampard’s side responded superbly after being hammered 5-0 by Brighton in their last home game, tightening up in midfield and defence and finding precisely Forest’s weak spots that Oliver Glasner has been unable so far to armour-plate. Taiwo Awoniyi, who was sent off during that defeat by Brighton, is absent serving the second leg of his three-match suspension and Hajii Wright and Aurele Amenda are still some way off returning. Tino Livramento pulled out of the England camp with injury and is likely to be sidelined for a while longer but Matthias Jaissle was more optimistic about his raft of other doubts: William Osula, Lewis Miley, Amar Dedic, club captain Dan Burn, Anthony Elanga and Jacob Ramsey.

#1404. Giving Youri Tielemans a £35m release clause looks like an error... Aston Villa toiling to a draw with Sunderland was more proof Unai Emery could do with a midfield controller in January, writes TOM COLLOMOSSE

Published: 12:22 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 14:14 EST, 21 November 2026

Whoever put that £35million release clause in Youri Tielemans’ contract has a heck of a lot to think about these days.

The Belgian midfielder left Aston Villa to join Manchester United last summer and though these are early days in his Old Trafford career, the move does not seem to be working out for anyone.

Unai Emery was distraught to lose Tielemans and against Sunderland, you could see why. Emery signed two central midfielders, Leon Goretzka and Joao Gomes, and has given more minutes to Ross Barkley.

None of the three gives him what Tielemans did and Villa may decide to move for another central player in January. Anything for a bit of cleverness in that part of the pitch.

Tielemans has struggled at United and it will be interesting to see what Mauricio Pochettino makes of him. He is no elite athlete and United supporters and pundits have criticised him because of it but he gave Emery what he craves above all else – control. Neither Gomes nor Goretzka has Tielemans’ passing range and Barkley looks more effective higher up the pitch.

With Sunderland sitting deep here, Villa desperately needed a player who could read the game and create angles like Tielemans. Without him, their passing was slow and predictable, against a Sunderland side without key men Dominic Ballard, Granit Xhaka and Brian Brobbey.

Sunderland's Nordi Mukiele stretches for the ball but nobody could find the breakthrough

Regis Le Bris saw his side pick up another point to follow their win over Chelsea before the international break - Sunderland now sit 18th

Their only chance in the first half here fell to Emi Buendia, who won the ball high then failed to chip the back-pedalling Robin Roefs. In the second half, Ian Maatsen and substitute Ibrahim Mbaye shot far too close to the Sunderland goalkeeper, who tipped over another effort from Barkley.

Villa have still not lost in the league since they were beaten here by Nottingham Forest in September but teams aiming for the Champions League should put away Sunderland at home. And after 150 Premier League games at the helm, nobody will know that better than Emery.

Buendia reached Aston Villa immortality last May when he scored in the Europa League final and now he has his own banner.

‘It’s Buendia, with a beauty, on the banks of the Bosphorus’ read the slogan in the Holte End.

They will never forget that 3-0 win over Freiburg here but it is alarming just how quickly the team has split apart since then. Six months have passed since Istanbul but only two of the starting XI from that night – Buendia and Torres – were in Unai Emery’s line-up here.

Emi Buendia is now the subject of a banner from Villa fans for his Europa League final heroics

Youri Tielemans scored a stunner in the Europa League final but is now at Man United

True, Matty Cash and Victor Lindelof were injured, while John McGinn was left on the bench, with one eye on Tuesday’s return to Istanbul to face Galatasaray in the Champions League. Boubacar Kamara missed the final through injury.

Still these are huge changes. For most of Emery’s first four years at Villa, every player knew his role and understood the kind of team they were. Now Villa find themselves learning on the job in a three-sided ground, due to the improvement work that leaves the North Stand empty.

Emery knows it too. ‘We have brought a significant number of new players to the squad, many of whom are still adapting to the demands of competing at the level we have worked so hard to establish ourselves at.

ASTON VILLA (4-2-3-1): Suzuki 6; Wan-Bissaka 6, Harwood-Bellis 6, Torres 7, Maatsen 6; Kamara 6, Goretzka 5 (Barkley 73, 6); Alysson 6, Buendia 6 (McGinn 60, 7), Manzambi 5 (Mbaye 60, 6); Jackson 6 (Madjo 73, 6).

SUNDERLAND (4-2-3-1): Roefs 7; Meunier 7, Mukiele 7, O’Nien 7, Reinildo 7; Ahoka 8, Sadiki 7; Hume 6, Le Fee 7, Talbi 7; Isidor 7 (Angulo 77, 6).

'It takes time, patience, hard work and belief.

‘That is why, now more than ever, we must stick together, trust the direction we are heading in and continue to get behind our players and staff. Results are hugely important but so is recognising the hard work and development that will help us keep moving forward.’

These days clubs like Sunderland cannot afford to wait for young talents to prove themselves in other European leagues.

A decade ago, clubs in the middle of the Premier League could sign players like that for relatively small sums. Now everyone in Europe knows how rich top flight clubs in England are and adjust their prices accordingly.

That is why Sunderland paid nearly £10million for Jules Ahoka even though he had barely played a senior game for Royal Antwerp.

On this evidence, the Black Cats have spent wisely yet again. Ahoka is quick, athletic and strong – exactly what is required in English football today – and his technique is tidy too. If he stays healthy, a bright future awaits.

#1403. Lionesses take step closer to World Cup but do not look like they can win it

England may have edged a step closer to booking their place at next summer’s Women’s World Cup but they do not yet look like a team who can win it.

This two-legged qualifying play-off with Greece was always going to be somewhat academic. Greece are ranked 58th in the world and have never qualified for a major tournament. But they could – and should – have taken the lead before England eventually broke the deadlock through Georgia Stanway just before half-time.

The goals flowed more freely in the second half, but Greece deservedly found the net themselves and are not yet out of the tie. There is every chance of the Lionesses winning the second leg in Leicester on Tuesday more comfortably, but not being able to put teams to the sword is exactly why they ended up in the play-offs in the first place.

The best teams are ruthless and unforgiving – and England did not display those traits here. They snatched at chances, and several players were guilty of firing wide. There were also defensive problems. Greece got in behind England’s back line too often and the goal they scored was far too easy for them.

“I think we made it [the game] a bit harder,” England manager Sarina Wiegman said. “Greece were very well prepared. They were very well organised and well disciplined. Of course I’m happy with the 3-1, I’m not happy with the one.

“We could have scored more goals, we should have. The final stage, the final pass needs to be better. I think we were a little bit in moments really good on the ball and in other moments not so good, and we could have made better decisions too. Lots of things to take from today.

“Sometimes we played really well, sometimes we were a bit sloppy, so sometimes we were a bit frustrated and I think that’s what you saw.”

Avoid defeat in the second leg and England will play the winners of Ukraine v Slovakia. Ukraine, whom the Lionesses beat 6-1 and 3-0 earlier in their campaign, have a 3-1 lead from their first leg. Perhaps the pedestrian nature of this game was partly because it felt inevitable England would win. They did enough to get over the line but still lacked a clinical edge.

It had been four months since they were thrashed 4-0 by Spain, a defeat which relegated them to the play-offs instead of automatic qualification. They had won every other game in their group before that capitulation, but with Spain topping the group on goal difference, England only had themselves to blame for not scoring more goals in their other fixtures. Breaking down ultra-defensive teams has long been an issue for this Wiegman side and they knew that was what they would be facing in this double-header against Greece.

It did not help that many of Wiegman’s players have been struggling for form in the Women’s Super League this season. Wiegman was also without the ever-reliable Lucy Bronze, who dropped out of the squad on Thursday because of injury. That meant Maya Le Tissier was handed a start at right-back while Laura Blindkilde Brown was preferred to Jess Park in the No 10 position.

Greece were far more open than many would have expected, with several gaps in their defence for England to exploit. They also created problems for themselves by insisting on playing out from the back.

Tonight’s hosts are yet to qualify for a major tournament and are expected to set up in a defensive shape. England defender Esme Morgan believes the squad are ready for a long night of breaking down a stubborn opposition.

She told a pre-match press conference: “It’s just about persistence and trying not to get drawn into being frustrated by the opposition. A really good example was the away game against Ukraine in qualifying. We couldn’t seem to break through in the first half - the keeper was making saves, we hit the woodwork - but the messaging at half-time was just to keep continuing because we were creating opportunities.

”Not to start snatching or taking shots from distance, just trusting in our style of play and our ability to find gaps. We came out for the second half and scored really quickly. It’s just about sticking to the plan and being patient.”

Erica Meg Parkinson, one of England’s new midfielders, was apparently named after Eric Cantona.

While Cantona still famously is proud of his kung fu kick, when he attacked an obnoxious Crystal Palace fan, Parkison is less enthused by football’s most famous case of breaking the fourth wall.

“My dad is a huge Man United fan so I was named after Eric Cantona,” Parkinson says. “It’s a pretty good player to be named after except for, you know, the karate kicks.

“My brother was named after Denis Law. I don’t think my mum had much of a say in the name so she was dragged into it, but it kind of worked out because we both play football now.”

The excellent Kathryn Batte has run the rule over potential alternatives to Lucy Bronze.

The 35-year-old right-back is out injured, but Ella Toone was called up in her place, rather than a direct replacement.

“Bronze, who is two appearances away from reaching 150 caps for her country, has picked up an injury and returned to Chelsea for treatment,” Batte writes.

“The Lionesses will be missing one of their most reliable players for the matches on Friday and Tuesday, but it gives Sarina Wiegman an opportunity to look at potential replacements for the future.

“Bronze, who has been an integral member of the team throughout Wiegman’s reign, turns 35 later this month. While she will be expected to be the first-choice right-back should England qualify for next year’s World Cup in Brazil, the lack of a recognised back-up has been an ongoing problem.”

Sarina Wiegman revealed that while dropping Toone was a difficult decision, the midfielder’s reaction left a lasting impression on the coaching staff.

“When I gave her the call, of course that was a hard call, but she took that straight away,” Wiegman said. “Of course she was very disappointed, but the first thing she did was say: ‘OK, I’m going to get back, I’m going to do that.’”Wiegman was particularly pleased with how Toone handled herself both on the pitch and in front of the media before her late recall.

“That answer in the game, also the way she spoke about it, I thought that was really good,” the head coach added. “And then getting everything ready, I think that really impressed me. Well done, I would say.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Greece vs England in the first leg of the 2027 Women’s World Cup play-offs.

The Lionesses kick off the two-legged tie tonight looking to secure a solid advantage ahead of Tuesday’s return tie at Leicester’s King Power Stadium. Although they finished level on points with group winners Spain, England’s goal difference sent them into the play-off path, setting up a first-ever senior meeting against a Greek side ranked 55 places below them in the FIFA rankings.

All eyes are on Sarina Wiegman’s selection choices following a turbulent week of squad news. The manager originally raised eyebrows last month by dropping Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly, stating bluntly that “the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch.”

Toone quickly accepted the setback. Speaking after starting in Manchester United’s victory over Liverpool, the midfielder insisted: “It’s about me now. I’ve got to keep working hard and use it as fuel to come back even better.”

That opportunity arrived sooner than expected. An injury sustained by right-back Lucy Bronze - described by Wiegman as “really small” - forced the defender to return to Chelsea for assessment. Wiegman immediately turned to Toone, who flew directly to Greece from Spain, where she had been running her own self-directed training block during the international window.

With 69 caps and 24 international goals to her name - including crucial strikes in the Euro 2022 final and the 2023 World Cup semi-final - Toone brings proven big-match experience back into the setup at a critical moment.

We will bring you all the build-up, confirmed team news, and live play-by-play coverage throughout the evening.

#1402. Arsenal’s big guns blow Lille away after the second string flop

There will be some games where Mikel Arteta has no choice but to tweak the XI, rest some tired legs and give his second-choice attackers the chance – although given the option he may wish to pick the same team every week.

The three big guns of his attack were primed and ready to come on in the next break in play when Arsenal at last broke through in this, their second Champions League league phase game of the season against some stubborn opposition from Ligue 1. Lille had sat deep against an Arsenal attack without Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz, and the French club were past the hour when it all finally broke.

That was a superb finish from Jurrien Timber who, with two touches, demonstrated that in the modern era even defenders are capable of the kind of moments of skill and composure that we once assumed were only within the capacity of the best attackers. He gave Arsenal the lead just as Mikel Arteta had decided he had seen enough from some of his second-choice attackers – Viktor Gyokeres, Noni Madueke and Mikel Merino. They had created some chances and at times looked promising, but as soon as the big three were on the difference was obvious.

The Arsenal players wore black armbands to mark the passing, aged 94, of Ken Friar, the club’s life vice-president. Even Arteta, no sentimentalist, insisted on beginning his press conference with a tribute.

For Arteta’s players, there will be a much bigger test than this one in Munich next week against Bayern. Arsenal have already won in Naples but a victory at Bayern would be significant beyond that. Since returning to the competition under Arteta in 2023, they have won all 12 home group-stage or league-phase matches, conceding just three goals.

Including knock-out games, Arsenal have conceded just eight goals in 20 home matches, keeping 15 clean sheets.

Four of those goals came in effective dead rubbers against PSV in the 2025 last-16 (after Arsenal won 7-1 in Eindhoven) and against Kairat Almaty in the final game of last season’s league phase.

So in home Champions League games that matter, they have conceded just four goals in 18 matches: Serge Gnarby and Harry Kane for Bayern in the 2024 quarter-final, Ousmane Dembele in the 2025 semi-final and Lennart Karl for Bayern in last season’s league phase.

Lille are considering legal ⁠action after defender Tiago Santos suffered a serious knee injury following an “uncontrolled and dangerous” tackle in Saturday’s match ‌against Le Havre.

Santos, 24, suffered a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament and meniscal tear in his right knee and was carried off the pitch on a stretcher after being tackled by Le Havre midfielder Amir Richardson during the first half of Lille’s 1-0 victory.

The referee gave a foul for the tackle but did not issue Richardson with a caution.

Lille said the ‌tackle merited ‌a red card ⁠and that they had asked the league’s governing body (LFP) to refer the matter to its disciplinary committee. The club are also seeking an explanation of ⁠the video review process undertaken by match officials.

“LOSC is exploring all possible legal avenues and reserves the right to take any legal action necessary to obtain compensation for its losses,” the ​club said. “It will support Tiago in ‌any steps he decides to take to defend his rights.”

Will Olivier Giroud receive a warm welcome back to the Emirates Stadium? The Frenchman spent six years as an Arsenal player but burned a few bridges when he left the club for Chelsea, and then celebrated wildly when Chelsea beat Arsenal in the Europa League final of 2019. Now 40, Giroud has shown remarkable longevity and is unquestionably one of the best strikers of his generation. But can he hurt this formidable Arsenal defence? It’s a tough ask.

Olivier Giroud back at the Emirates ❤️ https://t.co/TPBgcNDsVW

Arsenal pay tribute to one of the club’s greatest custodians this evening following the news of Ken Friar’s death aged 92. Friar worked in various roles at the club across more than 70 years, and a bridge from Drayton Park to Emirates Stadium is named in his honour.

A statue at the end of the bridge is a nod to the chance meeting the 11-year-old Friar had with Arsenal manager George Allison in 1945, while playing football outside Highbury with his friends.

As Sam Dean wrote earlier today, finishing the story: “Allison was so impressed by Friar’s enthusiasm that he told him to report to his office at 9am the next day. Friar did as he was instructed and his reward was a job offer: he became a messenger at the stadium on match days. He was paid 12 and a half pence per week.”

Friar was a long-serving member of the Arsenal board, before stepping back in 2020 and becoming life president.

Arsenal’s players will wear black armbands.

A post shared by Sam Dean (@samjdean_tel)

After signing his new Arsenal contract last week, Mikel Arteta described May’s Champions League final defeat as “poison in his veins,” and last season’s campaign demonstrated the benefits of finishing top of the league phase.

Arsenal enjoyed home second legs all the way through to the final after winning eight from eight, and in a 50:50 draw they fell into a considerably kinder bracket.

Sometimes it can be hard to gauge the importance of these league-phase matches, but Arteta will strive for another perfect record to give Arsenal the best possible chance of going deep in the competition again.

Fixtures against Bayern Munich and Real Madrid are likely to determine whether Arsenal finish in the top two, but there is still a job to be done against Lille this evening.

Arsenal have played against 10 different French opponents in European competition but have never faced Lille, who are managed by Davide Ancelotti, son of five-time Champions League winner Carlo.

Lille sell their best players every summer. After finishing third in Ligue 1 last season they lost Ayyoub Bouaddi and Matias Fernandez-Pardo to Manchester City and Newcastle United for a combined £130m. They have claimed 10 points from their first five league games of the season and led Paris St-Germain 2-0 before being pegged back in stoppage time.

Leading the line for Lille is 40-year-old Olivier Giroud, who scored 105 Arsenal goals in 235 appearances between 2012 and 2018. After leaving the Emirates, Giroud went on to score against Arsenal for Chelsea in the 2019 Europa League final, but he can still expect a warm reception.

Arsenal’s home record in the Champions League has been formidable since they returned to the competition under Arteta in 2023. They have won all 11 home group-stage or league-phase matches, conceding just three goals (two of those were shipped against Kairat Almaty in a dead rubber).

Arteta’s scope for rotation has been reduced by injuries to Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi, but tonight’s game should offer Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyokeres a chance to impress, while Jurrien Timber needs minutes to build his fitness.

#1401. Man City are failing to give their supporters something to stand behind as Enzo Maresca's side radiate uncertainty with meek display in Fulham draw, writes JACK GAUGHAN

Published: 11:04 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 14:16 EST, 21 November 2026

The bananas are disappearing now winter is coming, the fire and fury waning with each passing week. In legal limbo, Manchester City’s supporters need something – anything – to stand behind but increasingly their team refuse to provide that solace.

City were booed off at the end as Enzo Maresca ducked down the tunnel. Some of that could have been directed at referee Thomas Bramall, after Erling Haaland’s disallowed goal, but certainly a significant number were jeering what they’d just seen. That simply does not happen at the Etihad Stadium, even during the torrid run of two years ago.

But they are witnessing a squad who radiate uncertainty. Who take three touches when two will do; who always receive possession squarely facing their own goal; who do not create passing lines for their mates. And crucially, who are forever momentarily confused as to who exactly is picking up which runner and those split seconds make all the difference in this division.

There is just this strange state of unease around how they want to approach games at the moment, something that adversity can provoke and something that Maresca is adamant he can correct. A coach of his calibre should do given the time and freedom.

Yet when he spent the two-week international break studying clips and fashioning ways of improving, he cannot have envisaged a scenario whereby home fans were so incredulous at a lack of energy that they were roused to their feet when Haaland deigned to close down Bernd Leno and force an error.

Man City put in an underwhelming performance as they were held to a 1-1 draw by Fulham

Enzo Maresca's side are radiating uncertainty and look worryingly vulnerable at the back

Rodrigo Muniz made City pay as he put an impressive Fulham 1-0 ahead after 16 minutes

Fulham popped it about nicely and at will. Found pockets to hurt their illustrious hosts, who were again asking a centre half – in this case Marc Guehi – to charge into midfield. City did have more balance than at Nottingham Forest for including Ayyoub Bouaddi for Enzo Fernandez, yet Alvaro Arbeloa still aggressively pressed them in that area to some success.

‘I told the players that we will have the chance to beat them if we play with courage,’ said Arbeloa, who was indebted to the towering performance of defender David Affengruber.

Arsenal will have watched this grinning and could easily be racking up an unassailable lead once these teams meet in north London next Sunday. Unassailable with all the usual caveats about the appeal and what this season may or may not eventually mean.

City did create enough statistically but as with other games of late, that did not tell the whole story.

Calvin Bassey pirouetted through midfield, the heavily derided Gianluigi Donnarumma thwarting a number of strong Fulham chances, and City appeared somewhat lost and out of ideas.

Elliot Anderson equalised with a superb volley but City failed to create much after that

Maresca expressed his concern at City's lack of clean sheets after they struggled again

That is a worrying departure from recent defeats, where they attacked with the same abandon as that early season flourish when they might as well have hosted games at Madison Square Gardens and played with an orange ball.

MAN CITY (4-2-3-1): Donnarumma 7; Khusanov 6, Dias 6, Guehi 5, O’Reilly 5 (Gvardiol 78); Anderson 7, Bouaddi 7 (Fernandez 85); Ndiaye 6 (Allan 78), Foden 7 (Cherki 70), Doku 5; Haaland 5

FULHAM (4-2-3-1): Leno 6; Tete 6, Affengruber 8, Bassey 7, Sessegnon 7 (Palacios 83); Berge 6, Charles 7; Bobb 7 (Garcia 78), King 6 (Larsson 70, 6), Iwobi 7 (Robinson 70, 6); Muniz 7 (Cairney 83)

Met with a Fulham who had not conceded more than once in the league since the start of September, City failed to create a meaningful opportunity in the last 25 minutes of a match they were desperate to win and should have been in the ascendancy of after Elliot Anderson’s volleyed equaliser after half time.

Maresca, though, is more concerned with a lack of clean sheets. It’s now none of those in nine games in all competitions for the first time in seven years, with Rodrigo Muniz opening the scoring on 16 minutes. A throw inside Fulham’s own third prompted Guehi to jump and lose his duel, City turned around and Oscar Bobb laid on for Muniz.

‘We’re conceding too many goals,’ Maresca said. ‘We need to avoid it. You need to win games 1-0. You need clean sheets. We’re not able to do it. But I can see many positive aspects. We started four months ago and not four years ago.

‘We’ve conceded almost 80 per cent of our goals at the start of the first half and second half. It’s something we need to improve. It’s a throw in at the corner flag and nobody is expecting they can create something.’

Maresca was also insistent that Haaland ought to have been awarded an equaliser before the break when poking in on the goal line, yet Bramall adjudged that Leno had the ball under control on field, with VAR not overruling.

Some hard luck, some profligacy with Haaland squandering a couple of big chances, but the day was summed up when in stoppage time, Jeremy Doku was penalised for a foul throw.

#1400. TransA-MERFISH reveals divergent post-retinal direction-selective circuits

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

A major goal in neuroscience is to map the transformation of information as it flows through the brain. For example, neurons at many levels of the visual hierarchy are attuned to motion direction1,2,3,4,5. However, links between motion-selective computations and cell types at various stages of the visual hierarchy remain unidentified. A key first step in delineating these relationships is to map the wiring diagrams that connect different motion-selective cell types. Here we establish a systematic, cell-type-specific circuit-mapping method, combining an anterograde trans-neuronal fluorescent tracer (mWGA–mCherry)6 with spatial transcriptomics (multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH))7,8 to establish TransA-MERFISH. We used TransA-MERFISH to comprehensively map the synaptic target cell types of four retinal ganglion cell subclasses in superior colliculus (SC) at cell-type resolution. These experiments unexpectedly revealed that retinal on–off direction-selective ganglion cells (ooDSGCs) innervate several direction-selective SC cell types, but do not innervate a SC cell type that was previously reported to display strong direction-selective responses. We validated these results using orthogonal approaches and demonstrated the sensitivity and specificity of TransA-MERFISH. Functional studies of SC activity before and after ablation of retinal direction-selective circuits confirmed that these computationally distinct, ooDSGC-dependent and -independent direction-selective cell types are commingled in SC. Together, our study establishes TransA-MERFISH as a robust framework for mapping wiring diagrams at the cell-type level and uncovers divergent computational mechanisms of motion detection in early visual processing.

A central objective in neuroscience is to characterize the computational transformations that occur across successive nodes of neural circuits. In the visual system, this requires defining the mechanisms by which retinal signals are integrated and processed as they ascend to higher brain centres. Among these, motion signals are particularly salient, providing the sensory substrate for critical behaviours such as predatory pursuit, escape and spatial navigation9,10. Over the past half-century, neurons in various brain areas have been found to respond to visual motion. A particularly common form of motion sensitivity is a preference for stimuli moving in a certain direction, a property known as direction selectivity that is observed in the retina, SC and cortex1,2,3,4,5. However, relationships between direction-selective cell types in different brain areas are unknown, leaving equally unclear how direction-selective activity is used and transformed across different stages of the visual hierarchy. A key obstacle has been the lack of a wiring diagram to guide understanding of information flow between the tens of different retinal ganglion cell (RGC) types and similarly diverse neuronal cell types in target areas such as SC. Here, we describe the development of a technological platform that enabled us to address these knowledge gaps.

Efforts to map neural circuits have yielded a diverse array of methodologies, yet existing ‘gold-standard’ approaches face considerable scalability and molecular identification constraints. Although electron microscopy provides high-resolution reconstructions11,12,13,14, it remains incompatible with the molecular profiling of pre- and postsynaptic partners and is currently impractical for brain-wide mammalian applications. Similarly, physiological techniques such as channelrhodopsin-assisted circuit mapping (CRACM)12 and Patch-seq15,16 provide precise functional data but are limited by low throughput. Recent sequencing-based strategies (such as Retro-Seq, Project-Seq, VECTOR-Seq, MAPseq and BARseq)17,18,19,20,21 have advanced the field by using RNA barcodes to define projection targets of starter neurons at high throughput, but these strategies trace axonal projection targets in the brain, and do not identify their synaptic target cell types within those areas. Additionally, these methods often rely on tissue microdissection, thereby losing anatomical context. These limitations underscore the need for next-generation, readily adoptable methods for comprehensive connectivity mapping at cell-type resolution.

To fill this gap, with a particular focus on comprehensive mapping of synaptic target cell types, we integrated a genetically encoded anterograde fluorescent trans-neuronal tracer, mWGA–mCherry (mWmC)6, (Fig. 1a) with the spatial transcriptomics technology, MERFISH7,8 (Fig. 1b). This combined platform, which we named TransA-MERFISH, required two major technical advances. First, we established an experimental workflow that enables the combination of anterograde trans-neuronal tracer immunostaining and MERFISH-based spatial transcriptomics. Second, we developed an automated data processing pipeline to align connectivity and transcriptomic data—that is, to overlay fluorescent signals from anterograde tracers on the spatially resolved neural identity data derived from multiplexed RNA signals in MERFISH (Fig. 1c). We then applied TransA-MERFISH to investigate the aforementioned half-century-old unresolved problem in visual neuroscience: the relationship between direction-selective neuron types and computations at different stages of the visual hierarchy. We used TransA-MERFISH to establish a comprehensive, cell-type-resolution wiring diagram downstream of ooDSGCs, a well-studied RGC subclass attuned to stimuli moving in one of the four cardinal directions: nasal, temporal, dorsal or ventral22,23. Using Cre transgenic mice, we mapped the SC synaptic target cell types of ooDSGCs that prefer particular directions24,25,26. We unexpectedly found that although ooDSGCs strongly innervate several SC cell types, they do not innervate the cell type that a previous study27 claimed was most direction-selective in SC. These surprising results were validated using multiple genetic, anatomical and electrophysiological tests. Subsequent in vivo imaging studies of SC activity before and after ablation of retinal direction-selective circuits confirmed that computationally distinct ooDSGC-dependent and ooDSGC-independent direction-selective cell types are commingled in SC. Our research establishes TransA-MERFISH as a high-throughput approach for generating cell-type-level wiring diagrams and reveals divergent computational strategies for visual motion detection.

a–c, Schematic of the TransA-MERFISH workflow. a, AAV2-mWGA-mCherry is delivered to left retina for trans-neuronal transfer of mWmC from all RGCs onto retino-recipient neurons in right SC. b, At 4 weeks post-injection (wpi), sSC was imaged. c, A 140-gene panel was used to classify sSC neurons. Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq)-based methods have laid the groundwork for understanding neuronal taxonomy, including scRNA-seq studies covering the entire SC region28,29. However, these methods require tissue dissociation and microfluidics-based single-cell isolation, which reduce spatial resolution, the completeness of cell-type identification, and scalability for large-scale mapping. We therefore developed a preparation to combine anterograde trans-neuronal tracing with spatial transcriptomics (MERFISH). Because the established MERFISH protocol uses fresh-frozen tissue to maximize RNA preservation30,31, it is incompatible with immunostaining for protein markers such as the anterograde trans-neuronal tracer mWmC. Therefore, we developed a protocol to perform MERFISH on fixed tissue. To benchmark this protocol, we sought to create a reference atlas of SC neurons in the retino-recipient superficial SC (sSC) (Fig. 1c). We referred to existing scRNA-seq data6,19,28 to select 140 neuron-type marker genes to classify retino-recipient neurons in the superficial SC (sSC) (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Figs. 1e,f and 2f,i and Methods). We developed a perfusion–fixation MERFISH protocol that ensured that RNA integrity and neuronal morphology were not compromised compared with fresh-frozen tissue, while preserving protein localization (Extended Data Fig. 1a–d and Methods). We then performed MERFISH on sSC, followed by Cellpose-based segmentation (as in past MERFISH studies in the mouse brain31), which covered all sSC neurons (Fig. 1h,i and Methods). This pipeline classified sSC neurons into 8 excitatory cell types (ENC1–8, marked by Slc17a6) and 11 inhibitory cell types (INC1–11, marked by Gad1) (Fig. 1d–g and Extended Data Fig. 1g–j). Data quality for SC cell classification from the modified TransA-MERFISH protocol (Extended Data Fig. 3a–e) closely matched that of several published scRNA-seq datasets19,27,28 (Extended Data Fig. 2c,e–j), as well as the cell types and supertypes reported in the Allen Brain Atlas dataset30 (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). Together, these data validate the feasibility of performing MERFISH in fixed tissue.

Analysis of spatial distributions found that each ENC cluster is restricted to a specific sublamina along the dorsal–ventral axis (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 4f), consistent with past observations in rodents and zebrafish6,32,33,34. INC1, INC2, INC5 and INC6 are also restricted to specific sublaminae along the dorsal–ventral axis, whereas INC3, INC4 and INC7–11 are spread across multiple sublaminae (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 4g). In addition, we observed a consistent distribution of all ENCs and INCs along the anterior–posterior and medial–lateral axes, which largely follows the sublaminar arrangement, without layer swapping (Extended Data Fig. 4a–e). Collectively, the MERFISH data map the sublaminar distribution of sSC neurons along the dorsal–ventral axis at single-cell-type resolution. Each cluster is further compared and quantified in Extended Data Table 1.

Having established a MERFISH protocol compatible with immunostaining and created an atlas of sSC cell types, we next sought to overlay cell connectivity information onto it. To do so, adeno-associated virus (AAV) encoding mWmC was delivered to the left eye to yield nearly complete coverage across all RGC types (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 6a). mWmC protein was transferred anterogradely and monosynaptically to the synaptic targets of RGCs in the contralateral (right) sSC, which receives innervation from around 90% of RGCs35. We then performed MERFISH on fixed tissue followed by anti-RFP immunostaining on the same microscope to facilitate registration with the MERFISH data. As a result, mWmC signals identified by anti-RFP immunostaining could be clearly registered with the RNA-based Cellpose segmentation masks (Fig. 1i,j and Methods). All mWmC+ neurons in the SC downstream of a given RGC starter neuron could be captured by imaging approaches and molecularly identified using MERFISH. Based on co-registered mWmC signals and MERFISH transcripts, we established a computational pipeline to assign mWmC signals to segmented neurons at single-cell resolution, followed by manual proofreading (Fig. 1i,j and Methods). The optimized workflow enabled high-throughput registration. This computational pipeline determines the percentages of mWmC+ neurons within each neuronal cluster, providing a quantitative measure of connectivity at cell-type resolution (Fig. 1k and Methods). We termed this integrated workflow TransA-MERFISH because it combines anterograde trans-neuronal tracing with MERFISH-based cell classification to read out connectivity.

Using TransA-MERFISH, we examined the synaptic target cell types of all RGCs. Roughly half (49 ± 3%, mean ± s.e.m.) of sSC neurons had a detectable mWmC signal (Fig. 1k). Across sSC neuron types defined by MERFISH, 5 out of 8 ENCs and 6 out of 11 INCs were classified as retino-recipient neurons based on mWmC signals above baseline, including a cell type that we recently showed to be retino-recipient (Npnt+)6 (Figs. 1k and 2a,c and Extended Data Fig. 3f–h). Notably, multiple ENCs and INCs in the sSC did not receive mWmC and were therefore not categorized as recipient neurons of RGCs, including a cell type that was previously6 characterized as not retino-recipient (Etv1+) (Figs. 1k and 2c,o). These data thus suggest TransA-MERFISH possesses the sensitivity and specificity to map synaptic connectivity at scale.

The spatially resolved map of all retino-recipient neurons in SC (Fig. 2b) generated with TransA-MERFISh enabled direct comparison of connectivity across cell types within shared sublaminar contexts. Notably, several SC neuron pairs exhibited divergent RGC connectivity despite occupying similar sublaminar distributions (Figs. 1f and 2a,b,g–o). For example, in the most superficial SC, ENC1 and ENC2 neurons were retino-recipient, whereas neighbouring INC1 neurons were not; similarly, in slightly deeper layers, ENC5 and INC6 neurons received retinal input, whereas neighbouring ENC6 neurons did not. These observations suggested that sublaminar position alone is insufficient to explain synaptic targeting by RGC axons. To test whether molecular cell-type identity contributes to synaptic specificity beyond sublaminar organization, we implemented a permutation-based framework in which cell-type labels were randomly shuffled within depth bins along the dorsal–ventral axis (Fig. 2d and Methods). This procedure preserves the sublaminar distribution of mWmC labelling while disrupting the association between molecular identity and connectivity. Cell-type specificity was quantified by comparing observed mWmC enrichment or depletion for each cell type against the permutation-derived null distribution. Using this approach, we identified multiple retino-recipient clusters, including ENC1, ENC2 and ENC5, with significant enrichment of mWmC labelling after accounting for sublaminar positions (Fig. 2e). By contrast, multiple non-retino-recipient clusters, including INC1 and ENC6, characterized here, showed significant depletion relative to sublaminar expectations (Fig. 2e,p). Together, these results indicate that RGC axons innervate SC neurons in a cell-type-specific way rather than simply according to their sublaminar distributions; that is, molecular identity, rather than sublaminar distribution, determines wiring specificity from the retina to SC.

We validated the sensitivity and specificity of TransA-MERFISH using CRACM. We first examined ENC5, which corresponds to genetically labelled Npnt+ wide-field neurons6 (Extended Data Fig. 5i and Extended Data Table 1). ENC5 was known to receive strong RGC input: 54 ± 6% (mean ± s.e.m.) of Npnt+ neurons contained mWmC labelling (Fig. 1j,k). CRACM quantitatively validated the TransA-MERFISH prediction, with a comparable percentage (52 ± 2%, mean ± s.e.m.) of Npnt+ wide-field neurons innervated by RGCs (Extended Data Fig. 5a,b,d). By contrast, ENC6 neurons, marked by Etv1, were in the same sublamina as ENC5 but did not receive direct retinal input in the TransA-MERFISH data (Fig. 1k). Consistently, these neurons did not receive RGC input in CRACM experiments (Extended Data Fig. 5a,c,d). These results validated the finding that ENC5 neurons receive input from the retina, whereas ENC6 neurons are not innervated by RGCs (Extended Data Fig. 5e–h). Together, these data support the notion that TransA-MERFISH provides a high-throughput platform for quantitatively defining neuronal synaptic target cell types at cell-type resolution.

To demonstrate the power of TransA-MERFISH to enable the discovery of synaptic target cell types of genetically defined starter cells, we decoded synaptic target cell types in SC of four major RGC subclasses that detect distinct visual features36: αRGCs (Kcng4-cre); ooDSGCs (Cartpt-cre); F-RGCs (Foxp2-cre); and T5-RGCs (Tusc5-cre)24,37,38,39,40 (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 6). These parallel TransA-MERFISH experiments yielded a comprehensive connectivity matrix at cell-type resolution. We observed highly distinct synaptic target cell-type compositions for different RGC subclasses (Fig. 2g–n). For example, ENC5 (Npnt+) neurons receive input from αRGCs, but not from ooDSGCs, consistent with our CRACM and trans-neuronal tracing results, and ENC6 (Etv1+) neurons receive no input from any of the four RGC subclasses (Figs. 1k, 2f–n,p and Extended Data Fig. 7). In addition, because different RGC subclasses arborize in distinct sSC sublaminae, we sorted the synaptic target cell types by their sublaminar distributions and connectivity frequencies (Fig. 2b,h,j,l,n and Extended Data Fig. 7). We found that retino-recipient neurons largely share the sublaminar distributions of the axonal arbors from that RGC subclass. For example, robust connectivity was reported from αRGCs to ENC4 and ENC5 neurons in lower stratum griseum superficiale (SGS) and stratum opticum (SO) (Fig. 2g,h and Extended Data Fig. 7b), with αRGC axons primarily ramifying in the same sublaminae24,26,40,41 (Extended Data Fig. 6i). By contrast, ooDSGCs, F-RGCs and T5-RGCs primarily innervated superficial ENC1 and ENC2 (Fig. 2i–n and Extended Data Fig. 7b–f), correlated with their axons primarily innervating the upper SGS (Extended Data Fig. 6i). Collectively, the TransA-MERFISH data provided a detailed neuronal connectivity map from the retina to SC at the level of cell types, offering functional insights into parallel retinotectal circuit organization and further validating the sensitivity and specificity of this tool for mapping comprehensive connectomes in a high-throughput manner.

A notable finding emerged from analysis of the synaptic target cell types of Cartpt-cre-labelled RGCs, which are ooDSGCs that are reported to prefer upward (dorsal) or downward (ventral) motion24,42. Cartpt+ ooDSGCs innervated 3 ENC clusters (ENC1, ENC2 and ENC4) as well as 4 INC clusters (INC3, INC4, INC5 and INC9) (Figs. 2i,j and 3c). The strongest targets of ooDSGCs, ENC1 and ENC2, are excitatory clusters marked by Cdh7 (Figs. 1g and 3a–d and Extended Data Fig. 2d). They are in the most superficial 100 µm of SGS, commingled with INC1 neurons, which are marked by Cbln4 (Fig. 1g) and are negative for mWmC labelling (Fig. 3c,d). Notably, the permutation test on TransA-MERFISH data (Fig. 2d,e) also showed that ENC1 and ENC2 have the highest synaptic enrichment for innervation from the retina, whereas INC1 neurons have the lowest (Fig. 2e), emphasizing the importance of cell-type-specific molecular properties among these neuron clusters in recruiting ooDSGC input.

The lack of mWmC labelling from ooDSGCs in INC1 was unexpected, because a recent study combining calcium imaging with post hoc in situ hybridization found that Cbln4+ SC neurons were strongly direction-selective31. Moreover, other studies have suggested that SC direction selectivity depends on ooDSGCs43,44. Together, these results appear to predict that the strongly direction-selective Cbln4+ SC neurons would be innervated by ooDSGCs. Therefore, to verify these findings, we generated the FlpO knock-in lines Cdh7-FlpO (Fig. 3e–h, Extended Data Fig. 5j,k,p,q and Methods) and Cbln4-FlpO (Fig. 3i–l, Extended Data Fig. 5l–o and Methods), and performed CRACM, mWmC anterograde tracing and rabies retrograde tracing. All of these methods confirmed strong monosynaptic input from ooDSGCs to Cdh7+ SC neurons (Fig. 3m,n,r,s and Extended Data Fig. 8a–c,h,j,l) but not from ooDSGCs to Cbln4+ SC neurons (Fig. 3m,o,r,t and Extended Data Fig. 8d,e,i,j,m). Moreover, mWmC anterograde and rabies retrograde tracing found negligible input from RGCs in either the contralateral or ipsilateral eye to Cbln4+ SC neurons, and CRACM using all RGC expression of ChR2 did not detect monosynaptic input from contralateral RGCs to Cbln4+ SC neurons, consistent with the TransA-MERFISH data (Figs. 2a and 3p,q,u and Extended Data Fig. 8f,g,k,n,o). These experiments thus validate the unexpected finding from TransA-MERFISH that the strongly direction-selective Cbln4+ SC neurons are not innervated by ooDSGCs from either the contralateral or ipsilateral eye (Figs. 2f,i,j and 3q and Extended Data Fig. 8d,e,k,o). These results demonstrate the specificity and sensitivity of TransA-MERFISH for systematic synaptic target cell-type mapping, enabling biological discovery.

The preceding circuit tracing data suggested that Cdh7+ SC neurons may inherit their direction selectivity from ooDSGCs, whereas Cbln4+ SC neurons may not. A key functional prediction of this differential wiring is that the direction selectivity of Cdh7+ SC neurons depends on the retinal ooDSGC circuit, whereas that of Cbln4+ SC neurons does not. To test this prediction, we used two-photon calcium imaging (Fig. 4a,d,i,l) to analyse the direction selectivity of both SC cell types at baseline and after ablation of starburst amacrine cells (SACs), which reduces direction selectivity of ooDSGCs45 (Fig. 4b,c,j,k,q,r and Extended Data Fig. 9a–f). Consistent with predictions from our TransA-MERFISH experiments, SAC ablation reduced the direction selectivity of Cdh7+ SC neurons (Fig. 4c,f–h) but not of Cbln4+ SC neurons (Fig. 4k,n–p). We further examined the contribution of ipsilateral retinal ooDSGCs by covering the ipsilateral eye and ablating SACs bilaterally (Extended Data Fig. 9m,o) and found no changes in direction selectivity in Cbln4+ SC neurons (Extended Data Fig. 9n,p). These data indicate that the direction selectivity of Cbln4+ SC neurons is independent of retinal ooDSGCs, whereas Cdh7+ SC neurons inherit direction selectivity from retinal ooDSGCs. Together, these data support the notion that multiple mechanisms underlie computationally distinct direction selectivity across different SC neuron types, including retinal ooDSGC-dependent direction selectivity in Cdh7+ SC neurons and retinal ooDSGC-independent direction selectivity in Cbln4+ SC neurons. Analysis of the preferred directions of these two populations revealed another marked difference: in the imaged region of SC (posterior and medial), Cdh7+ SC neurons showed a broad distribution in preferred directions (Fig. 4q and Extended Data Fig. 9g–i), whereas Cbln4+ SC neurons preferred a very narrow distribution of direction, mainly preferring dorsal-to-nasal motion (Fig. 4r and Extended Data Fig. 9j–l). These differential population biases suggest that these neurons are likely to participate in distinct circuits (Fig. 4s).
